articles.title: Prevent Hallucinated Bot Commands: Build an LLM Tool Loop for Telegram in Node.js
articles.excerpt: When building a Telegram bot powered by a Large Language Model (LLM), developers often start by feeding the user's message directly to an inference API and piping the raw string output back to bot.sen…
articles.body: When building a Telegram bot powered by a Large Language Model (LLM), developers often start by feeding the user's message directly to an inference API and piping the raw string output back to bot.sendMessage() . This works fine for generic Q&A, but breaks down completely when the user asks the bot to execute a concrete action, such as "Check the status of order #9482" or "Book a table for 2 people at 7 PM". If you rely on prompt engineering alone—asking the LLM to return plain text or raw JSON formatted like {"action": "check_order", "id": 9482} —the system will inevitably fail in production.
articles.author: Serhii

articles.title: I checked whether my readers were real, and the answer was 44 wallets for 44 payments
articles.excerpt: For a month my Subnano dashboard showed payouts arriving and I treated that as proof that strangers were paying for my writing. It is not proof of anything. A payout record tells you money reached you…
articles.body: For a month my Subnano dashboard showed payouts arriving and I treated that as proof that strangers were paying for my writing. It is not proof of anything. A payout record tells you money reached you. It does not tell you who sent it, and if the same wallet sends it every time, you are looking at your own test loop with extra steps. So I did the only check that answers the question. I took every payout in the ledger, walked each one back to its send block, and read the sending account. Forty-four payouts, forty-four different Nano addresses, zero repeats. Why the payout record is not enough The platform credits a creator share. What lands in my wallet is a transfer from the platform, so every row looks identical: same sender, same memo shape, same amount.

articles.title: Your Coding Agent Knows the Rule. So Why Does It Keep Breaking It?
articles.excerpt: You tell Claude Code not to modify a particular interface. It acknowledges the instruction. It fixes the code. A few sessions later, it makes the same mistake again. You add a rule to CLAUDE.md. The a…
articles.body: You tell Claude Code not to modify a particular interface. It acknowledges the instruction. It fixes the code. A few sessions later, it makes the same mistake again. You add a rule to CLAUDE.md . The agent reads it. Everything looks good. Then it happens again. At some point, you start wondering whether your instruction file needs to be longer, more specific, or rewritten entirely. But what if the problem isn't the instruction itself? The problem with telling agents what to do Files like CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are useful. They give coding agents persistent context about a repository, its conventions, and how developers want work done. But they have a limitation: giving an agent a rule is not the same as getting it to follow that rule when it matters.

articles.excerpt: Astronomers have spotted a remarkable gamma-ray burst that's a real Incredible Hulk compared to other cosmic explosions of the same type.
articles.body: Astronomers have spotted a remarkable gamma-ray burst (GRB) that's a real Incredible Hulk compared to other cosmic explosions of the same type. What makes this GRB so special is the fact that the central engine powering it remained active for around 27 days, flaring in X-rays following the initial blast. That's 20 days longer than the longest previous GRB on record. This record-breaking burst — which is designated GRB 220706A and was spotted on July 6, 2022 — is even more exciting because scientists don't know what the central engine powering it actually is. "In a nutshell, GRB 220706A is an extremely late X-ray flare.
